extracted.intended_audience: students and novice journalists (writers learning journalistic practices)
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory guide to core journalistic practices and standards, covering ethics, newsworthiness, sourcing, structure (inverted pyramid), AP style, leads, and press-release drafting. Intended to orient students/new journalists to the conventions and purposes of news writing across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are expected to keep an objective mindset at all times as they interview sources, research events, and write and report their stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should not aim to persuade readers but instead to inform. Subjectivity should be confined to clearly labeled opinion-based content (editorials, columns, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gathering, recording, and verifying information
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism is the practice of gathering, recording, verifying, and reporting on information of public importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is an explicit part of the journalistic process; reporting should rely on accurate collection and confirmation of facts before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists devote most of their efforts to working with primary sources rather than relying on secondary or tertiary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interviews, eyewitness accounts, original documents, and first-hand reporting over encyclopedias or scholarly summaries when developing news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews and quotation use
rubrics_metrics.description: When researching and writing their story, journalists will often interview a number of individuals—from politicians to the average citizen—to gain insight into what people have experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes collected from interviews drive and shape news stories; use them to provide perspective, evidence, and human interest while ensuring accuracy and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media ethics (collecting and reporting information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics of collecting and reporting on information is a core journalistic standard addressed in the guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of ethical issues (e.g., fairness, privacy, harm, confidentiality, conflicts of interest) when obtaining and publishing information; follow established ethical practices outlined in the broader ethics guidance pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide includes an overview of 'The Components of "Newsworthiness"' as criteria for selecting and prioritizing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess potential stories against standard newsworthiness factors (timeliness, proximity, impact, prominence, conflict, novelty, human interest) to determine coverage priority — see the dedicated components page for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing convention: the inverted pyramid structure is highlighted as a core organizational method for news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most important facts and answers to who/what/when/where/why/how at the top (lead), with supporting details and background following; useful for clear, concise news presentation and for accommodating editing/trimming.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to write a lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide addresses 'How to Write a Lead' as a distinct element of news writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should quickly deliver the most critical information (often the key facts or the story's hook) and set the tone and scope for the piece; see the lead page for types and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated Press (AP) Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Associated Press (AP) Style is presented as a central writing convention for journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP Style for spelling, capitalization, abbreviation, numbers, attribution, and other common newsroom usage to ensure consistency and professionalism in news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release formatting and drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The site includes guidance on 'Writing Press Releases' — formatting and drafting journalistic content intended for distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases should be formatted and written to summarize news clearly and concisely, using appropriate structure, contact information, quotes, and boilerplate; see the press-release page for templates and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting to multiple media formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists today may produce text, film documentaries, podcasts, photo essays, 24-hour TV broadcasts, and social-media/internet content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to adapt reporting, storytelling techniques, and technical skills to the chosen medium (e.g., audio pacing for podcasts, visual composition for photo essays, concise copy for social media) while maintaining journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: inform the public to enable informed decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Collectively, journalistic media help members of the public learn what is happening in the world so they may make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize public-interest information and clarity; frame reporting to provide the facts and context necessary for readers/viewers/listeners to understand implications and act on information if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style guide and citation awareness (MLA/APA/Chicago overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists a 'Style Guide Overview' and references MLA, APA, and Chicago guides as part of subject-specific writing resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While AP Style governs much newsroom practice, be aware of and consult other academic/style guides (MLA, APA, Chicago) when appropriate (e.g., for citations, academic projects, or cross-purpose writing).
